related.en: fruit preserved in syrup, served to a guest
to treat a guest to food and drink

note:
A guest in Serbia (гостопри̏мство - hospitality) is traditionally welcomed (до̀чекати го̏ста) with respect and treated to food and drink (уго̏стити):
• coffee with Turkish delight
• homemade rakija with a snack and the toast «Жѝвели!»
• сла̀тко̄ (fruit preserve) with a glass of water
• on special occasions, bread and salt

Saying «осећај се као код куће» lets the guest know they are welcome here.
title: Serbian hospitality

related.en: The kum is no button (the role is an important one).

note:
A traditional wedding follows many rituals:
1. The wedding party (сва̑тови) comes for the bride (мла̑да).
2. The groom (младо̀жења) shoots at an apple placed high up in the yard.
3. A joking ransom; sometimes a "false bride" is brought out.
4. A ceremony in church and at the registry office.
5. The "who steps on the other's foot first" custom.
6. Carrying the bride over the threshold.

The newlyweds are младѐнци. The ку̑м has a special role, hence the saying «Ку̑м нѝје ду̀гме».
title: A Serbian wedding

note:
Serbs believe that a про̏маја (draft) is behind many ailments.

What people do and don't do:
• plan good things, then ку̏цнути у др̏во (knock on wood)
• don't звѝждати (whistle) at home
• don't sit on the corner of a table - you won't get married
• don't put a bag on the floor - you won't have any money

Other signs: an itchy left palm means money, bird droppings mean profit, and before an exam people pour water out behind the student.
title: Serbian superstitions

related.en: the main pedestrian street of Belgrade

note:
The main pedestrian street of Belgrade, Кнез Михаилова, is named after Prince (кне̑з) Mihailo Obrenović (born 2 October 1823).

What is linked with him:
• in 1867, under his rule, the Turkish garrisons peacefully left Serbian cities, including Kalemegdan
• he supported the building of the National Theatre (по̀зорӣште)
• he wrote poems, one of which became a well-known romance song

The monument to the prince on horseback (ко̏њ) in Republic Square is simply called «ко̏њ».
title: Prince Mihailo and Knez Mihailova Street

note:
Verbs with «се» fall into three groups:
• truly reflexive - the action is done to oneself: уми́вати се
• reciprocal - the action is done to each other, so two people are needed: сва̏ђати се
• reflexive in form only - a state or feeling, and the verb does not exist without «се»: смѐјати се

Another reciprocal verb: пољу́бити се (to kiss each other).
title: Three roles of the particle «се» with verbs

related.en: someone living in their own world

note:
Young Serbs take words from English and bend them to Serbian grammar. The words are not in textbooks, but on TikTok they are everywhere:
• флексовати (I flex - флексујем) - to show off
• кри̏нџ - something awkward
• делулу - someone living in their own world
• краш - a crush
• хајп - hype
title: Youth slang in Serbia

note:
A zodiac sign is хо̏роскопскӣ зна̑к. You can ask: «Ко̀јӣ си хо̏роскопскӣ зна̑к?»

The names of the signs:
• О́ван, Би̏к, Близа̀нци, Ра̏к
• Ла̏в, Дѐвица, Ва́га, Шкорпија
• Стре́лац, Ја̏рац, Водолија, Рибе

The ascendant is по̏дзнак, the natal chart is натална карта.
title: Zodiac signs in Serbian

note:
Many everyday words came from Turkish:
• џе̏зва, ко̀мшија, комшѝлук, шѐћер
• јо̏к - an emphatic «no»
• муштѐрија, фѝлџа̄н, ра́тлук, ра̀кија

After liberation from the Ottomans, Turkisms were fought against and some words disappeared, but many remain, and today they even help you read signs in Turkey.
title: Turkisms in everyday speech

related.en: a shot dropped into a beer

note:
Summer and bar drinks:
• шпри̏цер - wine with soda water
• гѐмишт - wine with mineral water
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola
• по̀дмо̄рница («submarine») - a shot of rakija dropped into a mug of beer
• бушена вотка - vodka with juice, from бу́шити - to drill

Шприцер and гемишт are often mixed up. Folk belief says ко̏ла helps with a hangover.
title: Summer and bar drinks

related.en: feast of a family's patron saint
boiled wheat with nuts and dried fruit

note:
Many Serbian families have a patron saint, whose day they celebrate as крсна слава. 19 December is Николин дан, so, as the joke goes, half of the Serbs celebrate a slava and the other half go to visit them.

On the table:
• славски колач - a round white bread
• славско жито or коливо - wheat with walnuts and dried fruit
• a candle and wine
title: Крсна слава - a family holiday

related.en: window (at a ticket office or post office)
to be lacking, to be missing

note:
During the Austro-Hungarian rule, many German words came into Serbian:
• фла̏ша, фле̏ка, ко̀фер, ке̏лнер, ша̀лтер
• штра̏јк, се̏нф, шпо̏рет, ко́рпа, та̏шна
• тѐпих, ве̏шмашӣна, ци̏мер
• капи́рати, фа̏лити
title: Germanisms in Serbian

note:
In messages, Serbs often write Latin script without the marks č, ć, š, ž, đ. Such Latin is called «bald» (ћелава) or «shorn» (ошишана).

Because of this, the meaning can change:
• ши̏ша̄ње (haircut) - си̏са̄ње (sucking)
• пошао (he went) - по̀сао (job)
• зна̏чи (means) - зна̑ци (signs)

For clarity, write with the diacritics or switch to Cyrillic.
title: Latin script without diacritics

related.en: to play a role, to act

note:
По̀зорӣште (theater) is formed from the verb зрети (to look), like про́зор (window), о̏бзӣр (attention) and прѐзирати (to despise).

Глу́мац (actor) goes with глу́мити (to play a role).
title: Where the word «позориште» comes from

note:
Cafe menus offer these sizes:
• кратка кафа - a ristretto, 20 ml
• дупла кафа - a double espresso made from two portions
• продужена кафа - one espresso with a lot of water (a lungo)

Montenegro also has «дојч кафа» - a lungo with warm milk, named after the German mark, to which its price was once equal.
title: Coffee: кратка, дупла and продужена

related.en: at the monument to Prince Mihailo
at the monument to Vuk Karadžić
the interchange of the highway to Niš

note:
Belgraders have their own names for places:
• «код коња» - the monument to Prince Mihailo in Republic Square
• «код Вука» - the monument to Vuk Karadžić in Zvezdara
• «круг двојке» - the loop of tram line 2 around the center
• «а̀уто-ко̀ма̄нда» - the interchange of the highway to Niš
• «у Двадесетдеветог» - Despot Stefan Street, formerly 29 November Street
title: Meeting places in Belgrade

related.en: slatko: fruit preserved in syrup, whole or in large pieces

note:
Guests in Serbia are traditionally greeted with a small plate of слатко and a glass of water - this is the добродо̀шлица.

Сла̀тко̄ is fruit preserved in syrup: figs, plums, sour cherries, quince. It is not quite jam: the fruit is whole or in large pieces.

How to accept the treat:
1. Eat a spoonful of слатко.
2. Wash it down with water.

Nowadays the custom survives mostly in the countryside.
title: Добродошлица: water and слатко

note:
The names of the legendary Yugoslav bands are literal. Here they are:
• Бијело дугме
• Забрањено пушење
• Екатарина Велика
• Пр̏љаво по̀зорӣште
• Рибља чорба
• Па̑рнӣ ва́љак
• Црвена јабука

The translations are in the related words.
title: Names of Yugoslav rock bands

related.en: a fair-haired woman with iron teeth, an evil spirit
a creature that weaves bast shoes from human sinews
«Steel Head», the counterpart of Koschei the Deathless

note:
Serbian mythology has many creepy characters:
• караконџула - a fair-haired woman with iron teeth; attacks in the «unbaptized days» between Christmas and Epiphany
• дрѐкавац - a howling creature, from the verb дречати
• ба̀ук - a clumsy monster; this is how «Shrek» was translated
• стухач - weaves bast shoes from human sinews
• Ба̏ш Чѐлик - the counterpart of Koschei the Deathless
title: Scary creatures of Serbian folklore

note:
In Serbia the seasons are counted by the astronomical calendar:
• зи́ма - until 20 March
• про̀леће - from 20 March to 20 June
• ле̏то - until 22 September
• је̏се̄н - after that

The answers to «when?»: зи̑ми, у про̀леће, ле̏ти, у је̏се̄н.
title: Seasons and «when?»

related.en: burek: a layered pastry pie (in Bosnia, only with meat)

note:
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, бурек means only a layered pie with meat. All the other kinds are пита:
• сирница - with cheese
• зељаница - with spinach
• кромпируша - with potatoes

In Serbia, Montenegro and Croatia it is simpler: «бурек са сиром», «бурек са спанаћем», «бурек са кромпиром».

The word itself came from Turkish.
title: Burek or pita?

note:
The language of the former Yugoslavia (except Slovenia and Macedonia) is based on the Shtokavian dialect. The dialects are named after the word «what»: што̏, ча̏, ка̏ј.

Today people speak of the Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin languages. In conversation, the diplomatic choice is «на̏ш јѐзик» (our language).

Once you have learned basic Serbian, you pick up the other variants with small differences in vocabulary and pronunciation.
title: What is the language called?

related.en: Božić Bata, the Serbian Christmas gift-bringer

note:
Several characters bring presents to children:
• Де̏да Мра̏з (Father Frost) - on New Year's Eve. He came to Yugoslavia from the USSR after World War II, while the Snow Maiden never caught on in the Balkans.
• Бо̀жић Ба̏та - on the night before Christmas, January 7.
• Saint Nicholas (Ни̏кољдан) - in December.

The figure of Божић Бата is gradually merging with Деда Мраз and Santa Claus.
title: Who brings presents in Serbia

related.en: hot rakija, the Serbian counterpart of mulled wine
«Šumadija tea», another name for hot rakija
džezva, a small pot for Turkish coffee

note:
The Serbian counterpart of mulled wine is куване ракије, or шумадијски чај. It is drunk hot in winter.

How it is made:
1. Melt шѐћер (sugar) into caramel in a џезва.
2. Add the rakija.
3. When it comes to a boil, add a little water.
title: Шумадијски чај: hot rakija

related.en: василица: a special bread for St Basil's Day

note:
The «Old New Year» by the Julian calendar is called Српска нова година or Српска Православна нова година among Serbs. It is celebrated on 14 January.

This day is Ма̏лӣ Бо̀жић, or Василијевдан - the feast of St Basil the Great. A special bread, the васѝлица, is baked.
title: Serbian New Year and Mali Božić

note:
For «happy» in greetings, Serbs say сре̏ћан: Сре̏ћан Бо̀жић, срећна нова година. Croats say сре̏тан.

This is one of the most noticeable markers of the variant. In Serbian text use сре̏ћан.
title: Срећан and сретан: Serbian and Croatian

related.en: to vibe, to be on the same wavelength
to ghost, to vanish without explanation

note:
Young people take English verbs and add Serbian endings:
• чиловати, кулѝрати - to chill
• вајбати - to vibe, to be on the same wavelength
• флексовати - to show off
• гоустовати - to ghost, to vanish without explanation
• кри̏нџ - secondhand embarrassment

Home-grown:
• «иде гас» - let's go, come on
• «скењ» - too bad, bummer
title: Zoomer slang in Serbian

note:
Сла̏вица on the Serbian internet is the counterpart of the Karen meme: a confrontational woman who lectures everyone about life.

Stickers also feature the fans of the Belgrade clubs:
• Делије - fans of Црвена звезда (Red Star), traditionally on the north stand
• Гробари - fans of Партизан, on the south stand
title: Славица, Делије and Гробари

related.en: Stefan Nemanja, the father of St Sava

note:
On 27 January Serbia commemorates Saint Sava - Савиндан. Sava was the first archbishop of the Serbian Church and the son of Stefan Nemanja.

This is the school slava: there are no classes in schools on this day.

What Sava is known for:
• he founded the Hilandar Monastery on Mount Athos
• he won independence for the Serbian Church in 1219
title: Савиндан - the school slava

related.en: a guy, a boy, a male (colloq.)
a woman, a girl, a female (colloq.)

related.sr: О̀ва̄ј ко̏њ је му̏шко, а о̀на је жѐнско.
related.en: This horse is a male, and she is a female.

note:
In colloquial speech, the words мушко and женско (in the neuter gender) stand in for мушка́рац (man) and жѐна (woman):
• «Буди мушко!»
• «Она је право женско.»

They are also used of a newborn: «Родила је женско.» (She had a girl.)

And of animals: instead of му̏жја̄к and же̑нка - «Овај коњ је мушко, а она је женско.»
title: Мушко and женско in the neuter

note:
Belgrade Fortress (твр̀ђава) and Калемегдан are not the same thing:
• the fortress - the fortifications themselves
• Калемегдан - the park around it, laid out in the 19th century

The name is Turkish: кале - fortress, мѐјда̄н - open field. Serbs themselves use both words as synonyms.

The Ри̑мскӣ бу̀на̄р was built by the Austrians in the 18th century.
title: Kalemegdan and the fortress

note:
Ту̀рбофолк arose in late Yugoslavia from the новокомпонована народна музика of the 1970s and flourished in the 90s.

Features:
• folk motifs combined with dance and electronic rhythms
• lyrics about love and infidelity
• a flashy aesthetic

The first stars were Lepa Brena, then Ceca. Wartime turbofolk is a separate patriotic subgenre.
title: Turbofolk

related.en: thick cream, similar to sour cream
a dairy product similar to sour cream

note:
Палачинке in Serbia are eaten both sweet and savory.

Savory fillings: ham and cheese, ground meat, salmon, caviar.

Sweet ones: nuts, almonds, coconut, шећер у праху (powdered sugar), jam, Nutella, еурокрем.

Close to sour cream here are па̀влака and милерам. One more topping is crushed «Plazma» biscuits.
title: Pancakes the Serbian way: fillings and toppings

related.en: the red Easter egg kept as a charm, the «house guardian»

note:
The first egg dyed for У̏скрс is red, and Serbs keep it until the next Easter. This is the чува̀ркућа - «house guardian»: according to belief, the egg protects the home and family.

It is not customary to throw it away after a year - better to bury it or throw it into running water.

The Easter greeting: «Христос васкрсе!» - «Ваистину васкрсе!»
title: Чуваркућа - the red Easter egg

related.en: SFRY, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes
FPRY, the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia
FR Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia

related.sr: Др̏жавна за̏једница Ср̀бије и Цр̏не Го̏ре
related.en: State Union of Serbia and Montenegro

note:
Yugoslavia changed its name several times:
• Краљевина Срба, Хрвата и Словенаца - 1918-1929
• Краљевина Југославија - until 1941
• ФНРЈ - 1945-1963
• СФРЈ - 1963-1992
• СР Југославија - 1992-2003 (Serbia and Montenegro)
• Државна заједница Србије и Црне Горе - 2003-2006

Then it broke up into independent countries.
title: How many Yugoslavias there were

related.en: Vuk Karadžić, the reformer of the Serbian language

related.sr: пи́ши ка̏о што̏ го̀ворӣш, а чи̏тај ка̏о што̏ је написа̀но
related.en: write as you speak, and read as it is written

note:
In the 18th century the Serbian literary language - славеносрпски - was a mix of Russian Church Slavonic and the spoken language. It differed greatly from the vernacular. Zaharija Orfelin and Milovan Vidaković wrote in it.

In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić rejected this and introduced the phonetic principle: «пиши као што говориш, а читај као што је написано» (write as you speak, and read as it is written).
title: Slavenoserbian and Vuk's reform

related.en: Бијело дугме, a Yugoslav rock band
«Time of the Gypsies», a film by Kusturica

note:
On 6 May Serbs celebrate St George's Day - Ђу̏рђевда̄н. It marks the coming of spring (про̀леће).

The song of the same name by the band Бијело дугме is linked with it. There are two versions of its origin:
• it was born in the war years
• it is a Serbian version of the Romani «Ederlezi», made by Goran Bregović for Kusturica's film «Вре́ме Ци̏га̄на» (Time of the Gypsies)
title: Ђурђевдан - 6 May

note:
In the Serbian translation the names are spelled the Serbian way: Хари Потер, Хогвортс, Волдемор.

Fun finds:
• нормалац - Muggle
• Смртождер - Death Eater
• Шѐшӣр за разврста́ва̄ње - the Sorting Hat
• Камен мудрости - the Philosopher's Stone
• Јецајућа Мирта - Moaning Myrtle
• ку̏ћнӣ вѝлењак - house-elf

A wizard is чаро̀бња̄к.
title: Harry Potter in Serbian

note:
Instead of «well», «um» and «like», Serbs insert па, о̀ва̄ј, да̏кле̄, зна̏чи.

Other filler words are often heard too:
• «како се зове», оно
• у фазону, бра̏те
• ре̏а̄лно, бу̏ква̄лно
• види, зна̑ш, ми̏слӣм

The English «by the way» is also in use.
title: Serbian filler words

note:
Видовдан is the day of St Vitus and the anniversary of the Battle of Kosovo in 1389, between Prince Lazar and the army of Sultan Murad.

The battle ended without a clear winner, but became part of the Serbian self-image and folklore.

Other events that fell on Видовдан:
• the assassination of Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo (1914)
• the Видовдански устав of 1921
title: Видовдан - 28 June

note: In many languages the «frog-eaters» are the French. In Serbian, жабари is the name for Italians: Italian cuisine also has frogs' legs.
title: Frog-eaters are Italians

related.en: Tear it, bro, I've become a dad!

note:
Serbs have a tradition: when a man has a baby, his friends tear his clothes (це́пати). It symbolizes his new status and is a wish for strength and happiness.

There are even T-shirts made for this - «мајице за цепање».

The friends shout: «Цепај, брале, постао сам ћале!»
title: Tearing the shirt of a new father

related.en: square pastries with meat or cheese

note:
Мантије are square pastries with meat or cheese, served with yogurt. They topped the TasteAtlas world ranking of savory baked goods. The Bosnian counterpart is буреџики (ranked lower).

Other Serbian pastries in the ranking:
• бу̀рек
• си́рница
• кромпируша
• зељаница
title: Мантије from Novi Pazar

related.en: festival of dishes baked under a сач (a bell-shaped lid covered with embers)

note:
The ending -ијада means a food festival:
• роштиљијада - grill, Leskovac
• сачијада - dishes baked under a сач
• сиријада - cheese
• купусијада - cabbage
• штрудлијада - strudel
• чваркијада - cracklings, Valjevo
• ракијада - rakija

In 2024 the Leskovac festival entered the Guinness Book of Records because of a huge пљескавица.
title: Festivals ending in -ијада

related.en: SANU, the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts

note:
Abbreviations are read out in full: нпр. - на пример, итд. - и тако даље, тј. - то јест, тзв. - такозвани, бр. - број.

Acronyms are read in different ways:
• as a word: МУП, САНУ, УНЕСКО
• letter by letter: РТС, СПЦ, ЕУ, САД
• in full: ОШ - основна школа

Some are indeclinable (члан САНУ), others take case endings (чланице НАТО-а).
title: Abbreviations and acronyms

note:
In Serbia Indian summer is called «михољско лето» after the feast of Михољдан (October 12). Real autumn is believed to begin after this date.

The feast is dedicated to St Cyriacus the Anchorite. The name may come from the Miracle of the Archangel Michael at Chonae, celebrated on September 19.
title: Михољско лето - the Serbian «Indian summer»

note:
Several dubs of the cartoon have come out across the former Yugoslavia, and the Serbian version differs from the Croatian one.

Vocabulary: су̀нђер (sponge), ко̏цка (cube), ли̏гња (squid), пѝпак (tentacle), кле́шта (claws), бѝсер (pearl), ко̀рал (coral), шко̑љка (shell).

The name Коцкалоне means «square pants»: ко̏цка + пантало́не.
title: SpongeBob in the Balkans

note:
The word «vampire» is of Slavic origin. It is believed to have entered the European languages specifically from Serbian.

Serbian folklore has many evil creatures, for example караконџула - an evil spirit.

A Halloween joke: dress up as a караконџула, that is, go to bed with wet hair.
title: Vampire and karakondžula

related.en: I do it for the pleasure of it

note:
Мѐра̄к is desire, enjoyment and unhurriedness: doing something without rush and with pleasure, even just drinking a cup of coffee or going to the shop.

The word is of Turkish origin, and it cannot be translated with a single word.

How people say it:
• «радим то из мерака»
• «нѝје ми мѐра̄к»
title: Мерак - Balkan pleasure

related.en: feast of a family's patron saint

note:
Сла̏ва is the feast of a family's patron saint. It lasts three days, and relatives and friends come.

How a guest behaves:
1. Don't come empty-handed: bring sweets, coffee, wine or rakija, flowers.
2. Congratulate the host: «Срећна слава, домаћине!»
3. Cross yourself, offer your congratulations and help yourself to the food.

The hostess may serve жи̏то - a ritual dish of wheat, walnuts and honey. The дома̀ћин begins all the rites.
title: How to behave at a slava

related.en: Children's Sunday, the third before Christmas
Mothers' Sunday, the second before Christmas
Fathers' Sunday, the last before Christmas

note:
On the three Sundays before Christmas, Serbia celebrates a family cycle:
• Детињци (the third Sunday) - adults symbolically tie up the children, who «ransom themselves» with a present, a song or a rhyme
• Материце (the second) - children tie their mother up with a ribbon, and she «ransoms herself» with sweets, nuts or small change; they give mum flowers and help around the house
• О̀ци (the Sunday before Christmas) - the same for fathers
title: Детињци, Материце, Оци

related.en: 5 January, the eve of Christmas Eve
Christmas roast piglet on a spit

note:
Туциндан is 5 January. The name is linked with the verb ту́ћи (to beat): on this day a young piglet is slaughtered for the Christmas dish - божићна печеница.

Beliefs:
• children must not be beaten on this day, or they will misbehave all year
• in some places, on the contrary, children are symbolically pulled by the ears

Legend: under the Turks, Serbs roasted pork specifically so that Muslims would keep away from the house.
title: Туциндан - 5 January

related.en: a shot of rakija in a mug of beer, «submarine»

note:
Home cocktails:
• шпри̏цер - white or rosé wine with soda water
• гѐмишт - wine with mineral water, but people more often call everything шприцер
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola
• по̀дмо̄рница («submarine») - a shot of rakija in a mug of beer
• бушена вотка - vodka with juice, from the verb бу́шити (to drill)

Cola is considered the best cure for a hangover.
title: Serbian home cocktails

related.en: popara: bread, cheese and a hot liquid
parizer: a boiled sausage like bologna

note:
What Balkan children eat:
• плазма with milk - biscuits soaked in milk; plazma is eaten in every form
• по̀пара - bread, cheese and a hot liquid
• па̀ризер - something like bologna, often with bread

Па̀ризер became a political joke: Vučić ate it during an election campaign to show he was close to the people.
title: What Balkan kids eat

note:
A common myth: Serbian words have no vowels.

In fact the sound «р» can be syllabic and take the place of a vowel: чвр̑ст, ср̏пскӣ, тр̏жӣште, цр̑в.

Mastering it takes practice and a trilled tongue tip; it is not a matter of swallowing vowels.
title: Syllabic R: Serbian is not a language without vowels

note:
On 14 February, besides Valentine's Day, Serbs celebrate Трифундан - the feast of Saint Tryphon, the patron of vine growers and winemakers.

On this day:
• the vines are pruned
• wine is drunk
title: Свети Трифун - 14 February

note:
The general word бу̏ба covers beetles and small insects.

The names:
• бубашва́ба - cockroach, «German bug»: the reddish-brown cockroach is thought to have come to the Balkans during the Austro-Turkish wars
• бубаруса - a related word, «Russian bug»: in popular speech, pests are often named after foreigners
• бубама́ра - ladybug, «Mary's bug», like the German Marienkäfer: it was linked with the Virgin Mary
title: Where insects get their names

note:
Names of the symbols:
• @ - мајмунско а or лу̑до а
• # - тараба
• $ - до̏ла̄р, % - по̀стотак, & - зна̑к «и»
• / - ко̀са цр̏та, \ - обрнута коса црта
• _ - доња црта
• ' - а̀построф, ; - та̏чка-за̀рез, : - двотачка
title: How to say @, # and other symbols in Serbian

note:
Easter (У̏скрс or Ва̏скрс) is prepared for in advance:
• Вѐликӣ пе́так - a strict fast
• Велика субота - eggs are dyed; the first, red one is the чува̀ркућа, which protects the home until the next Easter
• Sunday - after the liturgy people knock eggs together to see whose shell is stronger

People bake the bread погача, and only the eggs are blessed. The main dish is roast lamb.

Easter Monday is the time to visit people.
title: Easter in Serbia

note:
A Sarajevo story about the «Ѝна̄т ку̏ћа» - the «house of spite». When the Austro-Hungarian authorities were building the city hall on the bank of the Miljacka, they decided to demolish the house of old Benderija.

He refused and demanded:
• to be paid in ducats
• to have his house moved to the other bank - brick by brick

The authorities agreed, and the house was nicknamed Ѝна̄т ку̏ћа. Now there is a Bosnian restaurant there.
title: Инат кућа in Sarajevo

note:
At the market, nuts are sold by weight. The main names:
• о̀рах - walnut; it is also the tree
• ба́дем, ле̏шник, кикирѝки, пѝста̄ћ, пѝњоли

The rest are formed descriptively: индијски орах (cashew), бра̀зӣлскӣ о̀рах (Brazil nut).

Пекан, макадамија and ко̏кос sound as they do in English.
title: Nuts in Serbian
